clue.text: Traveller observant individual welcomes from a distance

indicators.note: a host who welcomes a guest takes them in, so the first piece lets the second inside it

parts.note: a seer is, read literally, one who sees: a person who notices things
afar means at or from a long way off, as in 'seen from afar'

explanation.surface: A watchful local waves a greeting to a wanderer who is still far off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcomes' has the observant individual take the distance word in, as a host would a guest. That individual is normally a prophet; the clue reads the word literally, as a person who sees.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a sailor journeys across the oceans for a living, so is one kind of voyager.

clue.text: Fish around bridge span opposite northwest bank?

parts.note: the bank facing the north-west one lies to the south-east, a compass point written as two initials
an arch is a single curved span of a bridge

explanation.surface: An angler casts about beneath the bridge, on the far side from the north-west shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks an invented phrase: a bridge's span at the end facing the north-west bank is its SE arch. The definition means to rummage, not to go angling.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to fish around, in a bag or for information, is to rummage or hunt for something.

clue.text: Part of bloom used by plant herbalist

indicators.note: used by says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A herbalist who works with plants makes use of one piece of a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Component: it is the pollen-bearing tip of a flower's stamen.

clue.text: Source of guilt as borstal is destroyed

indicators.note: something destroyed is smashed to pieces, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a borstal was a British detention centre for young offenders; here it is only letters

explanation.surface: Pulling down a youth prison leaves somebody with a troubled conscience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is destroyed' rearranges both words before it: the little word 'as' is fodder, not a link. In Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner the sailor must wear the bird he shot hung from his neck.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary idiom: in Coleridge's poem the seabird the mariner shot is hung from his neck, a lasting burden of remorse.

clue.text: Display unit by remarkable individual award-winner

indicators.note: by means beside, so the last piece is set down next to the two before it

parts.note: to display a painting in a gallery is to exhibit it
a unit is a single one, written as the Roman numeral I
a oner is informal British English for an outstanding person or thing, a one-off

explanation.surface: A shop's showcase stands next to an extraordinary prize-winning character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Display unit' reads as one piece of shop furniture but gives two pieces, and 'by' sets ONER after them. An exhibition is a British university scholarship, so its holder has won an award.
explanation.definitionFit: At British universities an exhibition is a minor scholarship, and the student who holds one bears this title.

clue.text: Undercoat for each skirting edge

indicators.note: to skirt something is to go round its outside, so the first piece passes round the second

parts.note: per means for each, as in miles per hour
the rim is the outer edge of a cup or a wheel

explanation.surface: A decorator needs a base layer of paint for the edge of every skirting board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirting' is a noun in the surface, the British name for a baseboard; as the container signal it is the verb for passing along the outside of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorating term: the preparatory paint brushed onto bare wood or metal before the finishing layers.

clue.text: Gunners brought in mostly to exert power over country

indicators.note: brought in says the gunners' abbreviation is carried inside the shortened word that follows
mostly means most of the word is kept, here all but its final letter

parts.note: to rule a people is to exert power over them
RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: Artillery troops are called up chiefly to keep a grip on the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' leaves RUL, and 'brought in' lodges the gunners' two letters in it. 'Country' poses as a noun, a nation, but the definition needs it as a describing word, as in country lanes.
explanation.definitionFit: Used attributively, as in country lanes or country life, it describes the farmland and villages away from towns.

clue.text: Possible prize fight — a case for the coppers?

parts.note: a prize may be a sum of money, hence 'possible'
to box is to fight with the fists in a ring

explanation.surface: A boxing bout that might be staged for a purse ends up as a matter for the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prize fight' is one phrase in the surface but splits into two pieces. 'Coppers' is British slang for police officers and also for low-value bronze coins; the definition wants the coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Punning description: coppers are British small-change coins, and this is the container children save them in.

clue.text: Strong attack removes bishop, by the way

indicators.note: removes says the bishop's abbreviation is taken away from the word for a strong attack

parts.note: a broadside is a fierce verbal attack, originally a warship firing all the guns along one flank at once
B is the chess notation for a bishop

explanation.surface: In a game of chess a powerful assault captures a bishop, the commentator adds in passing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removes' takes B from the front of BROADSIDE. In the surface 'by the way' is a casual aside; read literally it means beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal reading: 'way' is a road, so something beside the highway, like a verge or an inn, is described by this word.

clue.text: Stricken U-boat takes hours in a northern route to Germany

indicators.note: in places everything before it between the two single letters that come after it

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for north or northern, as in N Ireland

indicators.note: a stricken vessel is crippled and breaking up, so the letters of the word beside it are thrown out of order

parts.note: takes only joins this piece to the jumbled vessel; h is the abbreviation for hour or hours, as in 24h

explanation.surface: A crippled submarine spends hours limping home to Germany along a northerly course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stricken' makes UTOBA of the vessel; 'in' sets that and H between A and N. 'To Germany' is no destination: it means what Germans call such a road.
explanation.definitionFit: German loanword: it is what Germans call a motorway, their fast long-distance road.

clue.text: Managed to infiltrate spies in top compartments?

indicators.note: to infiltrate an organisation is to get inside it, so the word for managed slips within the spies

parts.note: the CIA is America's foreign intelligence agency, home of its spies
whoever ran a business managed it

explanation.surface: An agent succeeded in planting moles in the most secure sections of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to infiltrate' sends the word for managed into the spies. The question mark admits a playful definition: skulls are the body's uppermost boxes, the ones that hold the brain.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful description: these are skulls, the bony boxes at the head of the body that hold the brain.

clue.text: Bordeaux girl, say, I introduced to crafted German wine

parts.note: something crafted by hand was made

indicators.note: introduced to says the letter before it is brought into the two-piece run that follows

parts.note: Moselle is white wine from Germany's Moselle valley

explanation.surface: The speaker gave a young woman from France's wine country her first taste of an artisan German bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'introduced to' drops I into MADE MOSELLE. Bordeaux, a famous wine region, is here just a French city, and 'say' admits any French town would serve.
explanation.definitionFit: The French title for an unmarried young woman, of whom one from that city is an example.

clue.text: Event that's sure to include hard rock

indicators.note: to include something is to have it within, so the sure thing takes the next letter inside it

parts.note: a cert is British slang for a certainty, typically a horse bound to win its race
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A festival is guaranteed to have some loud guitar music on the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to include' puts H inside CERT. 'Hard rock' looks like one phrase, the loud music, but splits: 'hard' gives a letter and 'rock' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Geology term: a fine-grained sedimentary stone made of silica, of which flint is one variety.

clue.text: Carefully watch potential swarm circling garden walk

indicators.note: circling means going right round, so the insects' word surrounds the word for a garden walk

parts.note: bees are insects that may gather into a swarm, hence 'potential'
an alley is a path in a garden or park bordered by trees or hedges

explanation.surface: Keep a close lookout for what might become a swarm buzzing round the garden path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circling' sends the insects about the path. A garden walk is a path here, not a stroll, and 'potential' admits that these insects only sometimes swarm.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom for giving something your full visual attention, keeping a close lookout.

clue.text: Perhaps keep string round present just so things are clear

indicators.note: round means the first two pieces, taken as one run, go about the word for present

parts.note: a keep is the strongest tower of a castle, one kind of fort, hence 'perhaps'
cord is thin rope or thick string
someone present is here, as answered at a roll call

explanation.surface: Maybe hold on to the twine tied round a gift, simply so nothing gets muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' sends the first two pieces, as one run, about the third. In the surface 'keep' is a verb, to retain, and 'present' a gift; the wordplay wants a castle tower and being in attendance.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom said before a statement you want formally noted, to leave no doubt about where matters stand.

clue.text: A measure of effort so satisfied the queen

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore, used in English where one might say 'so'
an applicant who met the requirements satisfied them
ER, for Elizabeth Regina, was the royal cipher of Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: One piece of hard work pleased Her Majesty enormously.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So satisfied' reads as 'very pleased', but 'so' alone is ERGO, Latin for therefore. The definition is a gauge of work done, as fitted to rowing machines, not an amount of exertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Instrument sense of 'measure': a device, familiar from rowing machines, that gauges the work a body performs.

clue.text: Some will be divided by unattractive old plant

indicators.note: a word divided by others is split apart with them set in the gap, so the word for some opens up for the next two pieces

parts.note: any can mean some, as in 'have you any wool?'
grim describes a place or prospect that is bleak and unappealing
O is the abbreviation for old, as in OE for Old English

explanation.surface: A few people are bound to fall out over an ugly, ageing shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will be divided by' opens the word for some to admit the other two pieces. In the surface 'Some' is a few people falling out; here it is just a word to be parted.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanical name: a hedgerow herb of the rose family bearing spikes of small yellow flowers.

clue.text: Plant book has unusual alien in

parts.note: b is the abbreviation for book used in references and bibliographies

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the two words after it are put into a strange new order

explanation.surface: A gardening manual has an odd extraterrestrial lurking among its pages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' makes IENNIAL from the two words after it. The closing 'in' looks like an instruction to put something in the book, but one letter plus five is too short: 'in' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardening term: a species that lives two years and flowers in its second, such as a foxglove.

clue.text: Artist proceeds in the manner of sketches by Boz, mainly

indicators.note: by means beside: the piece from the words before it stands next to the shortened pen-name, after it

parts.note: the proceeds of a sale are the money it brings in, its gains

indicators.note: mainly means for the most part, so the pen-name is used without its final letter

parts.note: Boz was the pen-name under which Charles Dickens published his early pieces
sketches are rough drawings, quick and unfinished, so rough describes their manner

explanation.surface: A painter carries on in the style of Dickens's early writings, for the most part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sketches by Boz' is Dickens's first book, published under his pen-name; 'mainly' trims BOZ to BO and 'by' sets ROUGH beside it. 'proceeds' is the noun, takings, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gainsborough was an eighteenth-century English painter of portraits and landscapes, best known for The Blue Boy.

clue.text: Walk a little way to take the bus?

parts.note: a way is a street, and 'a little' shrinks it to its abbreviation St
to ride is to travel as a passenger, and a bus is one example of what you ride

explanation.surface: Somebody goes a short distance on foot to catch the bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little way' is not a short distance but a street cut down to its abbreviation. The question mark marks the bus as only one example of something you ride.
explanation.definitionFit: Type of gait: to go on foot with long, purposeful paces.

clue.text: Overlook furnace getting above temperature

indicators.note: in a down entry the piece getting above another is written first, higher up the grid

parts.note: a forge is the blacksmith's furnace where iron is heated for working
T is the physics symbol for temperature

explanation.surface: Someone fails to notice a furnace running hotter than it should.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting above' is a position in a down entry: FORGE sits on top of T. In the surface it reads as the furnace overheating.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to overlook a detail is to fail to remember or attend to it, to let it slip your mind.

clue.text: Hidden quality of a Scots city with very becoming name

indicators.note: becoming says one abbreviation turns into another inside the city's name

parts.note: Inverness is the main city of the Scottish Highlands
v is the abbreviation for very, as in 'v. good' on schoolwork
n is the abbreviation for name, as used on forms and in dictionaries

explanation.surface: A Scottish town with a most attractive name has a charm that visitors never notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming' turns the V of INVERNESS into N. In the surface 'becoming' is an adjective meaning attractive; here it is the verb that changes one letter to another.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of being inward or interior, so a characteristic kept out of sight.

clue.text: One pursues river horse — certainly not one of the big five

indicators.note: pursues means the piece from the word before it comes after the river and horse letters, chasing them

parts.note: R is the map abbreviation for river
horse and H are both slang names for heroin
one written as the Roman numeral I
an emphatic refusal is a plain no

explanation.surface: Someone hunts a hippo, an animal that is definitely not among the five great safari trophies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pursues' puts I after R and H. 'River horse' is the hippopotamus, which is no member of Africa's big five game animals; 'certainly not' is NO, leaving the rest as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Membership: Africa's big five game animals are lion, leopard, elephant, Cape buffalo and rhinoceros, whose short name this is.

clue.text: What's too much if wrapped in second piece of Xmas paper?

indicators.note: something wrapped in paper is enclosed by it, so the too-much abbreviation goes inside the word for a second

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second, as in 'half a mo'
OTT, short for over the top, is British slang for excessive

explanation.surface: Is it overdoing things to put a gift inside a second sheet of Christmas wrapping?
explanation.walkthrough: 'if wrapped in' sends the letters for over the top into the word for a moment. The definition is the slip of paper with a saying or joke on it that comes in a British Christmas cracker.
explanation.definitionFit: Specific sense: the slip printed with a saying or joke that is tucked inside a British Christmas cracker.

clue.text: Round drilling equipment in wellhead, perhaps

parts.note: the letter O is round in shape
a rig is the apparatus set up to drill for oil

explanation.surface: Somewhere around the drilling gear at the top of an oil well, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'in' that looks like a container signal is simply written out as the last two letters. A wellhead is also the source of a spring, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides the top of an oil well, a wellhead is the source of a spring, and figuratively where anything begins.

clue.text: Hard shoe lined with weak materials designed to wear

definitions.note: the definition is plural while the answer is a collective mass noun, much as 'belongings' could define 'luggage'

indicators.note: a lining sits on the inside, so the shoe has the word for weak fitted within it

parts.note: a clog is a shoe carved from wood or built on a rigid wooden sole
a thin excuse or a thin argument is a weak one

explanation.surface: A stiff shoe has an inner layer of flimsy fabric meant to be worn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lined with' gives the shoe an inner layer, the word for weak. 'Weak materials' reads as one phrase but divides: 'weak' is wordplay, while 'materials' begins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Collective noun for garments, the fabric items made for people to put on.

clue.text: Tree contains lines with ring showing signs of age

indicators.note: contains says the tree's name holds the next two pieces inside it

parts.note: the yew is an evergreen tree often found in British churchyards
l is the abbreviation for line, so two of them are lines
the letter O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A felled trunk holds lines and a ring that reveal how old the tree is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' has the tree hold the other two pieces. The surface suggests counting a trunk's growth rings; the definition is the colour old paper turns.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive sense: old paper and linen discolour to this shade over the years, so it marks something visibly aged.

clue.text: Bring up remainder book again

parts.note: to rear children is to bring them up
the rest is whatever remains, the remainder

explanation.surface: Somebody raises once more the matter of a title that was sold off cheaply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remainder book' looks like one phrase, a title sold off cheaply, but 'book' belongs to the definition: police book a suspect when they take them into custody.
explanation.definitionFit: Police slang: to book a suspect is to take them into custody and record the charge, and 'again' supplies the prefix meaning once more.
